What Is Bohemian Art Style? Origins and Core Characteristics

Bohemian art style traces its roots to 19th-century Europe, specifically to the Romani people of Bohemia (now the Czech Republic) and the unconventional artists and writers who adopted their free-living values. The word "bohemian" became synonymous with creative outsiders — people who collected art, travelled widely, and decorated their homes with objects from everywhere and nowhere in particular.

At its core, it's an aesthetic built on personal expression over perfection. There are no rules about matching, no pressure for everything to coordinate — just a commitment to surrounding yourself with things that mean something to you.

[[IMG|bohemian-art-style-origins-living-room|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, bohemian interior styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — macramé hangings, wooden shelves with plants and ceramics, hanging rattan lanterns. Scene: a warm, lived-in bohemian living room with terracotta walls, a low-slung sofa covered in layered kilim cushions and a chunky wool throw, a rattan coffee table holding stacked books and a large potted plant, mismatched ceramic vases on open wooden shelves, candles in various holders, warm golden afternoon light streaming through sheer curtains. Include a Black British woman in her mid-thirties sitting cross-legged on the sofa, relaxed, looking thoughtfully at something off-camera.]]

Core Characteristics of Bohemian Art Style

  • Layers of colour, pattern, and texture that feel collected rather than curated
  • A mix of cultures and continents — Moroccan, Indian, South American, African influences all appearing together
  • Natural and handmade materials: rattan, jute, macramé, wood, clay, leather
  • Plants — lots of them, in all sizes
  • Wall art and objects that tell a personal story
  • Low furniture, floor cushions, and a general sense of relaxed comfort
  • Warm, earthy tones anchored by jewel-toned accents
Pro Tip: The difference between a bohemian room that works and one that feels chaotic is intention. Even if the look is maximalist, every piece should feel chosen — not grabbed at random. Ask yourself: "Do I love this, or am I just filling space?"

Key Visual Elements of Bohemian Art: Colors, Patterns, and Textures

The visual language of bohemian art is rich, warm, and layered. Colours tend to run earthy and deep — think burnt sienna, ochre, forest green, dusty rose, indigo, and terracotta. Jewel tones like teal, ruby, and amber add depth without looking cold.

Patterns are equally important. Geometric prints, mandalas, ikat weaves, tribal motifs, and botanical illustrations all sit comfortably together in a bohemian scheme. The key is that no single pattern dominates — they coexist.

[[IMG|bohemian-colour-patterns-textures-flatlay|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Bohemian Art: Colours, Patterns & Textures". Then a clear VISUAL comparison with three labelled columns side by side: Column 1 "Colours" showing small paint-swatch-style circles in terracotta, ochre, indigo, dusty rose, forest green, and burnt sienna; Column 2 "Patterns" showing small labelled pattern swatches of geometric, ikat, mandala, and tribal motif; Column 3 "Textures" showing labelled close-up texture icons of rattan weave, macramé knots, rough-woven jute, and glazed ceramic. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Texture Is Everything

  • Layer smooth ceramics with rough-woven jute rugs
  • Mix metallic (brass, copper) with matte natural finishes (clay, unfinished wood)
  • Combine knotted macramé with printed cottons and velvet cushions
  • Use plants to introduce organic softness alongside harder surfaces
  • Wall art should include at least one tactile piece — a woven wall hanging, for example

I once helped a client in a Victorian terraced house in Bristol who kept buying beautiful individual pieces but couldn't understand why her room felt flat. The problem was she'd kept everything in similar textures — all smooth, all flat. We added a jute rug, a macramé wall hanging, and a hammered brass lamp, and the whole room woke up. Texture is what gives a bohemian room its life.

[[PRODUCT|bohemian mandala wall art prints]]
Pro Tip: Shop beyond home decor departments. Market finds, vintage fairs, and even craft shops are brilliant sources for genuinely textured, one-of-a-kind bohemian pieces.

Bohemian vs Boho-Chic vs Eclectic: What's Actually the Difference?

This is probably the question I get asked most often, so let me clear it up. These three terms overlap — but they are not the same thing, and understanding the distinction helps you shop and decorate with far more confidence.

Bohemian is the original aesthetic: unfiltered, maximalist, and rooted in a genuine mix of global cultures. Boho-chic is a more polished, commercially influenced evolution — it softens the rawness of true bohemian with cleaner lines and a more restrained colour palette. Think white linens, pampas grass, and carefully placed rattan chairs. It photographs beautifully but can feel a bit staged.

[[IMG|bohemian-vs-boho-chic-vs-eclectic-comparison|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Bohemian vs Boho-Chic vs Eclectic". Three clearly labelled columns side by side. Column 1 "Bohemian": labelled icon of a layered, maximalist room with global textiles, plants, candles, and macramé. Column 2 "Boho-Chic": labelled icon of a cleaner, more restrained room — white tones, pampas grass, rattan furniture, minimal clutter. Column 3 "Eclectic": labelled icon of a room mixing obviously different styles — a modern chair next to antique shelving, industrial lamp beside a floral rug. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Quick Comparison Table

Style Mood Colour Palette Key Feature
Bohemian Warm, maximalist, global Rich earthy + jewel tones Cultural mixing, plants, handmade objects
Boho-Chic Light, airy, polished Neutrals + muted pastels Cleaner lines, pampas, rattan
Eclectic Bold, deliberate, surprising Anything goes — intentionally Mixing different design eras and styles
Real Example: A client asked me for a "boho bedroom" but kept pinning images that were actually boho-chic — lots of white, dried flowers, and calm neutrals. Once she realised she wanted boho-chic rather than full bohemian, the brief became much clearer and the room came together quickly.

How to Incorporate Bohemian Art Style Into Your Home Decor

The good news is that you don't need to redecorate from scratch. Bohemian art style is genuinely one of the most accessible aesthetics to layer into an existing home, because it thrives on accumulation rather than starting over.

Start with your walls. A large-format wall print, a woven textile hanging, or even a small gallery arrangement immediately signals the style. Then build outward — add a layered rug, a plant or two, some mismatched cushions, and a couple of meaningful objects on a shelf.

[[IMG|bohemian-home-decor-living-room-styling|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, warm bohemian interior styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a large macramé wall hanging, wooden wall shelves with trailing plants and ceramic vases. Scene: a bright bohemian living room in a Victorian terraced house, with deep teal painted walls, a cream linen sofa loaded with layered kilim and embroidered cushions, a large vintage Persian-style rug in reds and golds, a rattan bookcase overflowing with plants and ceramics, brass candle holders on a low wooden coffee table. A South Asian woman in her early thirties is actively holding up two fabric cushion covers against the sofa, comparing them, with a warm, focused expression.]]

Simple Steps to Start Decorating with Boho Style

  • Hang a statement piece of wall art — a large botanical print or an abstract in earthy tones works brilliantly
  • Layer two or three rugs of different sizes and patterns
  • Add at least one tactile wall element: macramé, a woven hanging, or a wall-mounted shelf with trailing plants
  • Group ceramics and candles together on surfaces — odd numbers feel more natural
  • Introduce plants at different heights: hanging, shelf-level, and floor-standing
  • Use warm-toned lighting: amber bulbs, rattan lampshades, candles
  • Bring in at least one piece from another culture — a Moroccan lantern, an Indian block-print cushion, an African-inspired basket
[[PRODUCT|bohemian botanical wall art prints]] [[PRODUCT|rattan floor lamp for boho living room]]
Pro Tip: Don't buy everything at once. Bohemian rooms look best when they've been built up over time — it shows in the room's personality. Buy one or two meaningful pieces at a time and let the space evolve.

Bohemian Wall Decor Ideas by Room Type

One thing I rarely see discussed online is how bohemian wall decor ideas should adapt depending on which room you're decorating. What works brilliantly in a living room can feel overwhelming in a bathroom, and a bedroom needs a different energy to a kitchen.

So let me break this down room by room, because I think it makes the whole thing far less daunting.

[[IMG|bohemian-wall-decor-ideas-bedroom|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, warm bohemian interior styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — macramé wall hanging above the bed, wall-mounted brass sconces with warm-toned bulbs, a wooden floating shelf holding succulents and small ceramic pots. Scene: a cosy bohemian bedroom with dusty rose walls, a low-profile wooden bed with layers of linen, velvet and printed cotton bedding in terracotta and sage, a large trailing potted plant in the corner, a rattan bedside table with a stack of books and a candle, warm amber lamplight. A mixed-race couple — a man and a woman — are sitting up in bed, the woman reading, the man smiling at her, both relaxed and cosy.]]

Room-by-Room Bohemian Wall Decor Guide

  • Living room: Go bold — a large-scale wall hanging or a full gallery wall anchors the space. Mix prints, macramé, and open shelving with plants and ceramics
  • Bedroom: Keep it sensory but calming. A macramé headboard hanging, a couple of botanical prints, and wall-mounted sconces create warmth without overwhelm
  • Kitchen: Think practical and decorative — hanging bundles of dried herbs, a small gallery of food-related prints, and open shelving with handmade ceramics
  • Bathroom: One bold print, some hanging dried botanicals, and a rattan mirror are all you need. Keep it simple — bathrooms don't need much to feel bohemian
  • Home office: An inspiring wall print, a pinboard wrapped in fabric, and a trailing plant on a shelf keeps the energy creative and grounding
  • Children's room: Animal illustrations, a colourful woven wall hanging, and a few floating shelves with small plants (high up and child-safe) work beautifully
[[PRODUCT|boho wall art prints for the bedroom]]
Pro Tip: In smaller rooms like bathrooms, one single strong piece does more work than several small ones. Choose a print or hanging that makes you stop and smile every morning — that's worth more than a wall full of filler.

Types of Bohemian Wall Art: Prints, Tapestries, Macramé, and More

Bohemian wall art is wonderfully varied — it's not just prints. The real magic of this style is how different types of wall art coexist on the same wall without it feeling messy.

Here are the main types you should know about and how to use each one well.

[[IMG|bohemian-wall-art-types-macrame-tapestry|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, warm bohemian interior styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a large cream macramé wall hanging with long knotted fringe, a woven tapestry in terracotta and rust tones, wooden wall-mounted hooks holding hanging dried botanicals, a brass sunburst mirror. Scene: a wide bohemian living room wall styled with a mix of wall-hung textiles, a brass sunburst mirror, wooden floating shelves with trailing pothos plants and ceramic pots, warm golden side lighting. A tall Black British man in his late twenties is standing back and looking at the wall arrangement with an evaluating expression, one hand on his chin.]]

Bohemian Wall Art Types and When to Use Them

  • Art prints: The most versatile option — botanical illustrations, abstract earthy prints, and global-pattern designs all work. Great for gallery walls
  • Tapestries: Soft, large-scale, and incredibly effective for adding colour and pattern to a bare wall quickly. Particularly good in rental homes where you can't paint
  • Macramé wall hangings: Handmade-feeling and textural — perfect above a bed or sofa as a focal point
  • Woven wall art: Smaller and more detailed than tapestries — great for corners and alongside prints in a gallery arrangement
  • Ceramic wall art: Handmade-looking ceramic wall plates or sculptural clay pieces add an earthy, one-of-a-kind quality
  • Mirrors: A brass sunburst or hammered-metal mirror adds light, warmth, and depth — works brilliantly in dark corners
  • Hanging plants: An often-overlooked wall element — a hanging planter with a trailing plant is genuinely one of the easiest ways to add bohemian warmth to a wall
[[PRODUCT|boho tapestry wall art and woven prints]]
Pro Tip: Mix at least two types of wall art on any significant wall — say a print alongside a macramé hanging. The contrast in texture and material is what makes a bohemian wall feel genuinely layered rather than just decorated.

Colour Palette Planning for a Bohemian Gallery Wall

Gallery walls are one of the most popular bohemian decorating choices — but they go wrong surprisingly often. The most common mistake I see is people buying pieces they love individually, only to find they look like a jumble sale when hung together.

The fix is simple: plan your colour palette first, then shop within it. A bohemian gallery wall doesn't need to be matchy-matchy, but it does need a unifying thread.

[[IMG|bohemian-gallery-wall-colour-palette-planning|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, warm bohemian interior styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls on the actual wall — the wall itself is being styled live. Scene: a close-up of a large white living room wall with paint swatch cards, fabric swatches in terracotta, ochre, indigo and dusty rose, and printed paper mock-ups of potential wall art arrangements laid out on the floor in front of the wall, alongside small ceramic objects and a trailing plant cutting used to test the look. A South-East Asian woman in her early forties is crouching on the floor holding a terracotta paint swatch up to the wall, comparing it thoughtfully with the fabric swatches around her.]]

Colour Palette Planning Steps

  • Choose one anchor colour — often a warm neutral like terracotta, cream, or warm white — and use this as your wall colour or the most dominant tone in your art
  • Pick two to three accent colours that complement it: for example, terracotta + indigo + ochre is a classic bohemian combination
  • Include one or two neutrals (cream, sand, natural wood tones) to give the eye somewhere to rest
  • Keep frame colours consistent — natural wood, raw brass, or unframed all work; just pick one approach
  • Before buying, lay potential pieces out on the floor to check they work together
  • Include at least one textural piece (macramé, ceramic wall plate, woven piece) among the flat prints
Real Example: I helped a couple in Manchester plan a gallery wall above their dining table. They'd already bought four prints in completely different colour families. We removed two, kept the terracotta botanical print and the indigo geometric, then added a macramé hanging and a small brass mirror that picked up tones from both. The result was cohesive without looking matchy at all.

Boho Style in Dark Rooms: Making It Work

A lot of people assume bohemian style only works in bright, light-filled rooms — but honestly, boho style in dark rooms can be spectacular. Dark rooms suit the warm, moody, candlelit quality of a full bohemian scheme far better than a cool minimal aesthetic ever would.

The trick is to lean into the darkness rather than fight it, and use colour and light strategically.

[[IMG|boho-style-dark-room-interior|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, bohemian interior styling in a dark, moody room. Natural and warm artificial light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — macramé hanging, wooden shelves with trailing plants and ceramics, brass wall sconces with warm amber light. Scene: a dark, cosy bohemian living room with deep forest green painted walls, a velvet sofa in burnt orange with layered cushions in jewel tones, a large Moroccan-style rug in reds and golds, brass candleholders on every surface, warm amber wall sconces casting a golden glow, trailing pothos plants on shelves, a large terracotta vase on the floor. A white British woman in her early fifties is sitting on the sofa with a glass of red wine, completely relaxed, smiling softly at something off-camera.]]

Tips for Boho Style in Dark Rooms

  • Lean into deep wall colours — forest green, midnight blue, and charcoal all work brilliantly with bohemian textiles
  • Layer warm lighting generously: wall sconces, table lamps with amber bulbs, candlelight, and string lights
  • Choose wall art with warm tones — terracotta, gold, rust, and cream stand out beautifully against dark walls
  • Use mirrors to bounce light around — a brass sunburst mirror or a hammered-metal round mirror adds both light and style
  • Keep plants — they add life and freshness that stops a dark room feeling oppressive
  • Go for tactile textures: velvet, wool, and thick-woven rugs feel even more luxurious in a dark space
[[PRODUCT|warm-toned bohemian wall art prints for dark walls]] [[PRODUCT|brass sunburst mirror for bohemian room]]
Pro Tip: If you're worried a dark wall will make your room feel smaller, place a large mirror directly opposite the main light source. It doubles the perceived depth of the room and makes the warm lighting feel twice as golden.

Cohesive Boho Aesthetic Tips: How to Avoid the Jumble Trap

Getting cohesive boho aesthetic tips right is probably the most useful thing I can offer you in this guide. Because the number one complaint I hear is: "I've bought all this beautiful stuff and my room just looks messy." I completely understand — and there's a clear reason it happens.

Bohemian style celebrates abundance, but abundance without structure just becomes clutter. The key is to build in a few quiet rules that hold everything together without stifling the creative energy.

[[IMG|cohesive-boho-aesthetic-tips-living-room|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, warm cohesive bohemian interior styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a single large macramé wall hanging as a focal point, wooden wall shelves neatly styled with plants, ceramics, and books. Scene: a well-composed bohemian living room that feels layered but intentional — terracotta walls, a cream linen sofa with kilim cushions in a consistent terracotta, ochre and indigo palette, a jute rug layered over a printed cotton rug, plants at three different heights, ceramics grouped in odd numbers on a low wooden sideboard, warm side lighting. A young mixed-race couple, a man and a woman in their late twenties, are laughing together while rearranging cushions on the sofa, surrounded by the finished-looking room.]]

Cohesive Boho Aesthetic: Rules That Actually Help

  • Stick to a colour family: You can have many different pieces, but keep them within the same warm palette — earthy + jewel tones, or neutrals + botanicals, for example
  • Repeat materials: If you have rattan in one piece, echo it in another. Repeating materials creates visual rhythm
  • Use odd numbers: Group objects in threes and fives — it looks far more natural than even numbers
  • Create anchor points: A large rug, a statement wall hanging, or a sofa grounds the room so smaller pieces can build around it
  • Edit ruthlessly: Bohemian doesn't mean keeping everything. If a piece doesn't fit the palette or story, put it away
  • Leave negative space: Even in a maximalist room, the eye needs somewhere to rest. Not every surface needs to be full
Pro Tip: Before adding anything new, do the "remove one thing" test. Take one item out of the room and see if it looks better. If it does, that item was clutter. This habit alone transforms a room from jumbled to cohesive.

Buying Guidance and Product Pairings for Boho Art

Knowing what to buy and how to pair pieces together is where most people get stuck. It's easy to fall in love with individual items online, but harder to know if they'll actually work together in real life.

Here's how I approach it with my clients: I always start with the wall art, then build the room around it. The wall art sets the colour palette, the mood, and the cultural direction of the whole space.

[[IMG|buying-guidance-boho-wall-art-pairing|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, warm bohemian interior styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — macramé hanging, open wooden shelving with ceramics and trailing plants. Scene: a bright bohemian living room corner styled as a finished vignette — a low rattan armchair with layered cushions in ochre and terracotta, a jute rug, a tall potted fiddle-leaf fig beside the chair, a rattan side table holding a stack of books and a small brass candle lantern, wooden shelves on the wall with ceramic pots and trailing plants. A white British man in his late thirties is sitting in the rattan armchair, looking relaxed, holding a small decorative ceramic object and examining it with a warm, curious expression.]]

Smart Product Pairings for a Bohemian Room

  • Wall art print + macramé hanging: Pair a flat botanical or abstract print with a woven or macramé piece hung nearby — the contrast in texture works brilliantly
  • Wall art + jute or woven rug: Echo warm tones in both — if your print has terracotta, make sure your rug carries it too
  • Tapestry + floor cushions: A large tapestry as a backdrop makes floor cushions feel intentional, not afterthought
  • Ceramic wall plates + ceramic vases: Repeating the material between wall and surface ties a room together without being matchy
  • Brass mirror + brass candle holders: Repeating the metal finish unifies a space. Use brass sparingly but consistently
  • Abstract wall print + rattan furniture: A bold print adds colour; the rattan keeps the room grounded and natural
[[PRODUCT|abstract earthy wall art prints for bohemian living room]] [[PRODUCT|jute rug for bohemian living room]] [[PRODUCT|terracotta ceramic plant pots for boho decor]]
Pro Tip: When buying wall art online, download the image and use a free phone app to virtually place it on your wall before purchasing. It takes about two minutes and will save you a lot of returns.

Top Bohemian Artists and Influences to Know

Understanding the artists and movements that shaped bohemian art style gives you a much better eye for what genuinely fits the aesthetic — and what's just a trend pretending to be boho.

Key Influences on Bohemian Art Style

  • William Morris (UK): The Arts and Crafts movement's celebration of handmade beauty and natural botanical pattern is deeply embedded in bohemian style
  • Frida Kahlo (Mexico): Her embrace of folk art, vivid colour, personal symbolism, and cultural pride is quintessentially bohemian in spirit
  • The Pre-Raphaelites (UK): Rich colour, romantic nature scenes, and decorative detail — all major bohemian touchstones
  • Indian folk and textile arts: Block printing, ikat weaving, and hand-painted patterns from Rajasthan have deeply influenced the bohemian aesthetic globally
  • Moroccan and North African craft traditions: Geometric tilework, hand-knotted rugs, and hammered metalwork are foundational to the bohemian home
  • Contemporary boho illustrators: Modern botanical illustrators, watercolour artists, and abstract painters working with earthy palettes carry the tradition forward
Pro Tip: When shopping for wall art, look for pieces that feel handmade or hand-drawn — even if they're printed reproductions. That quality of human mark-making is what gives bohemian art its warmth. If it looks too digital or slick, it probably won't sit well in a boho scheme.

Bohemian art style is a free-spirited, layered approach to decorating that draws on global influences, natural materials, rich colour, and an anything-goes attitude to pattern and texture — and it's one of the most popular and misunderstood interior aesthetics around right now.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever walked into a room that felt warm, collected, and completely alive — with wall art stacked against shelves of trailing plants, woven textiles draped over a battered sofa, and candles flickering on every surface — and thought, "I want my home to feel exactly like this"? That feeling has a name, and it's bohemian.

Quick answer: Bohemian art style is an eclectic, globally inspired aesthetic that layers rich colours, natural textures, handmade objects, and culturally diverse patterns. It rejects minimalism in favour of personal expression and warmth. At home, it shows up in wall art, textiles, ceramics, and collections that tell a story.

The term gets thrown around a lot, but it genuinely means something specific — and once you understand it, decorating with it becomes much easier. In this guide I'll walk you through what bohemian art style actually is, where it comes from, and how to use it confidently in your home. If you're looking for unique wall art or unique home decor that fits this aesthetic, you're in exactly the right place.

What Is Bohemian Art Style? Origins and Core Characteristics

Bohemian art style traces its roots to 19th-century Europe, specifically to the Romani people of Bohemia (now the Czech Republic) and the unconventional artists and writers who adopted their free-living values. The word "bohemian" became synonymous with creative outsiders — people who collected art, travelled widely, and decorated their homes with objects from everywhere and nowhere in particular.

At its core, it's an aesthetic built on personal expression over perfection. There are no rules about matching, no pressure for everything to coordinate — just a commitment to surrounding yourself with things that mean something to you.

Core Characteristics of Bohemian Art Style

  • Layers of colour, pattern, and texture that feel collected rather than curated
  • A mix of cultures and continents — Moroccan, Indian, South American, African influences all appearing together
  • Natural and handmade materials: rattan, jute, macramé, wood, clay, leather
  • Plants — lots of them, in all sizes
  • Wall art and objects that tell a personal story
  • Low furniture, floor cushions, and a general sense of relaxed comfort
  • Warm, earthy tones anchored by jewel-toned accents
Pro Tip: The difference between a bohemian room that works and one that feels chaotic is intention. Even if the look is maximalist, every piece should feel chosen — not grabbed at random. Ask yourself: "Do I love this, or am I just filling space?"

Key Visual Elements of Bohemian Art: Colors, Patterns, and Textures

The visual language of bohemian art is rich, warm, and layered. Colours tend to run earthy and deep — think burnt sienna, ochre, forest green, dusty rose, indigo, and terracotta. Jewel tones like teal, ruby, and amber add depth without looking cold.

Patterns are equally important. Geometric prints, mandalas, ikat weaves, tribal motifs, and botanical illustrations all sit comfortably together in a bohemian scheme. The key is that no single pattern dominates — they coexist.

Texture Is Everything

  • Layer smooth ceramics with rough-woven jute rugs
  • Mix metallic (brass, copper) with matte natural finishes (clay, unfinished wood)
  • Combine knotted macramé with printed cottons and velvet cushions
  • Use plants to introduce organic softness alongside harder surfaces
  • Wall art should include at least one tactile piece — a woven wall hanging, for example

I once helped a client in a Victorian terraced house in Bristol who kept buying beautiful individual pieces but couldn't understand why her room felt flat. The problem was she'd kept everything in similar textures — all smooth, all flat. We added a jute rug, a macramé wall hanging, and a hammered brass lamp, and the whole room woke up. Texture is what gives a bohemian room its life.

Bohemian vs Boho-Chic vs Eclectic: What's Actually the Difference?

This is probably the question I get asked most often, so let me clear it up. These three terms overlap — but they are not the same thing, and understanding the distinction helps you shop and decorate with far more confidence.

Bohemian is the original aesthetic: unfiltered, maximalist, and rooted in a genuine mix of global cultures. Boho-chic is a more polished, commercially influenced evolution — it softens the rawness of true bohemian with cleaner lines and a more restrained colour palette. Think white linens, pampas grass, and carefully placed rattan chairs. It photographs beautifully but can feel a bit staged.

Eclectic Bold, deliberate, surprising Anything goes — intentionally Mixing different design eras and styles

How to Incorporate Bohemian Art Style Into Your Home Decor

The good news is that you don't need to redecorate from scratch. Bohemian art style is genuinely one of the most accessible aesthetics to layer into an existing home, because it thrives on accumulation rather than starting over.

Start with your walls. A large-format wall print, a woven textile hanging, or even a small gallery arrangement immediately signals the style. Then build outward — add a layered rug, a plant or two, some mismatched cushions, and a couple of meaningful objects on a shelf.

Simple Steps to Start Decorating with Boho Style

  • Hang a statement piece of wall art — a large botanical print or an abstract in earthy tones works brilliantly
  • Layer two or three rugs of different sizes and patterns
  • Add at least one tactile wall element: macramé, a woven hanging, or a wall-mounted shelf with trailing plants
  • Group ceramics and candles together on surfaces — odd numbers feel more natural
  • Introduce plants at different heights: hanging, shelf-level, and floor-standing
  • Use warm-toned lighting: amber bulbs, rattan lampshades, candles
  • Bring in at least one piece from another culture — a Moroccan lantern, an Indian block-print cushion, an African-inspired basket

Bohemian Wall Decor Ideas by Room Type

One thing I rarely see discussed online is how bohemian wall decor ideas should adapt depending on which room you're decorating. What works brilliantly in a living room can feel overwhelming in a bathroom, and a bedroom needs a different energy to a kitchen.

So let me break this down room by room, because I think it makes the whole thing far less daunting.

Room-by-Room Bohemian Wall Decor Guide

  • Living room: Go bold — a large-scale wall hanging or a full gallery wall anchors the space. Mix prints, macramé, and open shelving with plants and ceramics
  • Bedroom: Keep it sensory but calming. A macramé headboard hanging, a couple of botanical prints, and wall-mounted sconces create warmth without overwhelm
  • Kitchen: Think practical and decorative — hanging bundles of dried herbs, a small gallery of food-related prints, and open shelving with handmade ceramics
  • Bathroom: One bold print, some hanging dried botanicals, and a rattan mirror are all you need. Keep it simple — bathrooms don't need much to feel bohemian
  • Home office: An inspiring wall print, a pinboard wrapped in fabric, and a trailing plant on a shelf keeps the energy creative and grounding
  • Children's room: Animal illustrations, a colourful woven wall hanging, and a few floating shelves with small plants (high up and child-safe) work beautifully

Types of Bohemian Wall Art: Prints, Tapestries, Macramé, and More

Bohemian wall art is wonderfully varied — it's not just prints. The real magic of this style is how different types of wall art coexist on the same wall without it feeling messy.

Here are the main types you should know about and how to use each one well.

Bohemian Wall Art Types and When to Use Them

  • Art prints: The most versatile option — botanical illustrations, abstract earthy prints, and global-pattern designs all work. Great for gallery walls
  • Tapestries: Soft, large-scale, and incredibly effective for adding colour and pattern to a bare wall quickly. Particularly good in rental homes where you can't paint
  • Macramé wall hangings: Handmade-feeling and textural — perfect above a bed or sofa as a focal point
  • Woven wall art: Smaller and more detailed than tapestries — great for corners and alongside prints in a gallery arrangement
  • Ceramic wall art: Handmade-looking ceramic wall plates or sculptural clay pieces add an earthy, one-of-a-kind quality
  • Mirrors: A brass sunburst or hammered-metal mirror adds light, warmth, and depth — works brilliantly in dark corners
  • Hanging plants: An often-overlooked wall element — a hanging planter with a trailing plant is genuinely one of the easiest ways to add bohemian warmth to a wall

Pro Tip: Mix at least two types of wall art on any significant wall — say a print alongside a macramé hanging. The contrast in texture and material is what makes a bohemian wall feel genuinely layered rather than just decorated.

Colour Palette Planning for a Bohemian Gallery Wall

Gallery walls are one of the most popular bohemian decorating choices — but they go wrong surprisingly often. The most common mistake I see is people buying pieces they love individually, only to find they look like a jumble sale when hung together.

The fix is simple: plan your colour palette first, then shop within it. A bohemian gallery wall doesn't need to be matchy-matchy, but it does need a unifying thread.

Colour Palette Planning Steps

  • Choose one anchor colour — often a warm neutral like terracotta, cream, or warm white — and use this as your wall colour or the most dominant tone in your art
  • Pick two to three accent colours that complement it: for example, terracotta + indigo + ochre is a classic bohemian combination
  • Include one or two neutrals (cream, sand, natural wood tones) to give the eye somewhere to rest
  • Keep frame colours consistent — natural wood, raw brass, or unframed all work; just pick one approach
  • Before buying, lay potential pieces out on the floor to check they work together
  • Include at least one textural piece (macramé, ceramic wall plate, woven piece) among the flat prints
Real Example: I helped a couple in Manchester plan a gallery wall above their dining table. They'd already bought four prints in completely different colour families. We removed two, kept the terracotta botanical print and the indigo geometric, then added a macramé hanging and a small brass mirror that picked up tones from both. The result was cohesive without looking matchy at all.

Boho Style in Dark Rooms: Making It Work

A lot of people assume bohemian style only works in bright, light-filled rooms — but honestly, boho style in dark rooms can be spectacular. Dark rooms suit the warm, moody, candlelit quality of a full bohemian scheme far better than a cool minimal aesthetic ever would.

The trick is to lean into the darkness rather than fight it, and use colour and light strategically.

Tips for Boho Style in Dark Rooms

  • Lean into deep wall colours — forest green, midnight blue, and charcoal all work brilliantly with bohemian textiles
  • Layer warm lighting generously: wall sconces, table lamps with amber bulbs, candlelight, and string lights
  • Choose wall art with warm tones — terracotta, gold, rust, and cream stand out beautifully against dark walls
  • Use mirrors to bounce light around — a brass sunburst mirror or a hammered-metal round mirror adds both light and style
  • Keep plants — they add life and freshness that stops a dark room feeling oppressive
  • Go for tactile textures: velvet, wool, and thick-woven rugs feel even more luxurious in a dark space

Cohesive Boho Aesthetic Tips: How to Avoid the Jumble Trap

Getting cohesive boho aesthetic tips right is probably the most useful thing I can offer you in this guide. Because the number one complaint I hear is: "I've bought all this beautiful stuff and my room just looks messy." I completely understand — and there's a clear reason it happens.

Bohemian style celebrates abundance, but abundance without structure just becomes clutter. The key is to build in a few quiet rules that hold everything together without stifling the creative energy.

Cohesive Boho Aesthetic: Rules That Actually Help

  • Stick to a colour family: You can have many different pieces, but keep them within the same warm palette — earthy + jewel tones, or neutrals + botanicals, for example
  • Repeat materials: If you have rattan in one piece, echo it in another. Repeating materials creates visual rhythm
  • Use odd numbers: Group objects in threes and fives — it looks far more natural than even numbers
  • Create anchor points: A large rug, a statement wall hanging, or a sofa grounds the room so smaller pieces can build around it
  • Edit ruthlessly: Bohemian doesn't mean keeping everything. If a piece doesn't fit the palette or story, put it away
  • Leave negative space: Even in a maximalist room, the eye needs somewhere to rest. Not every surface needs to be full
Pro Tip: Before adding anything new, do the "remove one thing" test. Take one item out of the room and see if it looks better. If it does, that item was clutter. This habit alone transforms a room from jumbled to cohesive.

Buying Guidance and Product Pairings for Boho Art

Knowing what to buy and how to pair pieces together is where most people get stuck. It's easy to fall in love with individual items online, but harder to know if they'll actually work together in real life.

Here's how I approach it with my clients: I always start with the wall art, then build the room around it. The wall art sets the colour palette, the mood, and the cultural direction of the whole space.

Smart Product Pairings for a Bohemian Room

  • Wall art print + macramé hanging: Pair a flat botanical or abstract print with a woven or macramé piece hung nearby — the contrast in texture works brilliantly
  • Wall art + jute or woven rug: Echo warm tones in both — if your print has terracotta, make sure your rug carries it too
  • Tapestry + floor cushions: A large tapestry as a backdrop makes floor cushions feel intentional, not afterthought
  • Ceramic wall plates + ceramic vases: Repeating the material between wall and surface ties a room together without being matchy
  • Brass mirror + brass candle holders: Repeating the metal finish unifies a space. Use brass sparingly but consistently
  • Abstract wall print + rattan furniture: A bold print adds colour; the rattan keeps the room grounded and natural

Creating a feature wall in a grey room is one of the best decisions you can make for your home — grey is endlessly versatile, and a well-chosen feature wall can transform a flat, forgettable space into something that feels genuinely designed and intentional.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in your grey room, stared at four identical walls, and thought "something is missing here — but I have no idea what"? I hear this all the time from readers and clients alike. The good news is that the right wall art or feature wall treatment can be the single change that pulls everything together.

Quick answer: A feature wall in a grey room works best when you contrast tone, texture, or colour against your existing grey — think deep charcoal panels behind a sofa, warm-toned wallpaper in a bedroom, or a bold gallery wall of curated prints. Choose a wall that naturally draws the eye, then layer in complementary decor to give the space depth and personality.

A feature wall is simply one wall in a room that is treated differently to the others — through paint, wallpaper, panelling, or art — to create a focal point. When you're working with a grey room, that focal point becomes especially powerful because grey is such a neutral base; it plays well with almost any colour or texture you throw at it. If you're looking for unique wall art to anchor that feature wall, or unique home decor to style around it, the options are genuinely exciting once you know what you're doing.

Best Feature Wall Ideas for a Grey Room

The most successful feature wall in a grey room is one that creates contrast without clashing — and there are more ways to do that than most people realise. You don't have to go dark or dramatic; sometimes a textured finish in a warmer grey is all it takes to make one wall feel special.

The wall you choose matters as much as what you put on it. Almost always, I'd point you to the wall that your eye naturally lands on when you walk into the room — usually the one opposite the door, or the wall behind a sofa or bed.

Top feature wall ideas for grey rooms

  • Contrast paint: Go one or two shades deeper on the feature wall — a mid-grey room suits a near-black or slate feature wall beautifully.
  • Patterned wallpaper: A botanical, geometric, or textural wallpaper in warm tones (ochre, terracotta, blush) lifts grey brilliantly.
  • Vertical shiplap or panelling: White or off-white painted panels on a grey wall add architecture without competing.
  • Gallery wall of mixed prints: A curated collection of framed artwork creates the feature without any structural work at all.
  • Limewash or textured plaster effect: Adds organic warmth and depth to a grey room that can otherwise feel clinical.
  • Velvet or fabric panels: Unusual but increasingly popular — especially in bedrooms for warmth and acoustic softening.
Pro Tip: Before committing to any feature wall treatment, tape a large piece of paper or card to the wall and live with the colour or material sample for 48 hours. Grey rooms shift dramatically between morning light and evening lamplight, and what looks perfect at noon can feel completely different at 7pm.

Choosing Wall Art Colours and Styles for Grey Feature Walls

Wall art on a grey feature wall works best when it either warms up the grey (think earthy yellows, burnt oranges, terracotta, warm whites) or leans into the cool palette with deep navy, forest green, or charcoal tones for a moodier look. The key is choosing a direction and committing to it rather than mixing warm and cool tones at random.

Style matters too. I find that abstract art and line drawings work incredibly well against grey because grey doesn't compete with detailed artwork the way a busy wallpaper might. Photographic prints — particularly black and white or sepia-toned landscapes — are another reliable choice that feels timeless rather than trendy.

Best art colours and styles by grey shade

  • Warm grey walls: Pair with terracotta, rust, blush, or gold-toned artwork for a cohesive, earthy palette.
  • Cool grey walls: Try navy, forest green, dusty blue, or black-and-white prints for a crisp, contemporary feel.
  • Charcoal feature walls: Pale, airy artwork (cream backgrounds, light botanicals, soft abstract) creates beautiful contrast.
  • Light grey feature walls: Almost anything works — this is where you can be bold with deep jewel tones or vivid colour-block prints.
  • Abstract art: Works in almost every grey room because it adds energy without introducing a competing pattern.
  • Line art / minimalist prints: Ideal if you want the wall decor to feel considered but not overpowering.
  • Landscape and nature photography: Softens grey rooms beautifully — particularly moody coastal or woodland scenes.

I once helped a client who had a cool-toned dove grey living room and kept adding warm accessories that felt "off" no matter what she tried. When we looked closely, we realised her grey had a blue undertone, and her cushions and prints were all peachy-warm. We swapped the artwork for a pair of deep navy abstract prints, and suddenly every other element in the room fell into place. Undertones are everything.

Pro Tip: Hold a white piece of paper next to your grey wall in natural daylight. The wall will appear to shift — if it looks slightly blue or purple beside the white, it's cool-toned; if it looks slightly beige or pink, it's warm-toned. This tells you exactly which art colours will harmonise with it.

Wall art types that work best on grey feature walls

  • Large-format single prints: One oversized piece (think 60cm x 90cm or bigger) makes an instant statement on a grey feature wall and avoids the "nothing's happening here" problem.
  • Gallery wall sets: A curated set of 4–6 prints in a consistent colour story looks intentional rather than random. Keep frames consistent — all black, all natural wood, or all white.
  • Abstract art in warm tones: Earthy brushstroke prints, splashy watercolour abstracts in ochre and terracotta, or ink wash pieces bring warmth that grey alone can't provide.
  • Typographic prints: Work brilliantly in hallways and home offices against grey — particularly in bold black or deep navy on a cream background.
  • Photographic art: Moody landscape photography, architectural close-ups, or botanical macro shots suit the calm, considered feeling grey rooms tend to have.
Real Example: A client of mine had a large grey chimney breast in her Victorian terrace — it was the room's natural focal point but felt bare and imposing. We hung a triptych of oversized abstract prints in warm stone and slate tones, echoing the grey but adding texture and warmth. The room completely changed character. The chimney breast went from awkward to intentional in an afternoon.

Light Grey and Dark Grey Walls: How Tone Changes Everything

One of the questions I get most often is whether to go light or dark with a grey feature wall — and honestly, the answer depends entirely on the size and light levels of your room. Light grey and dark grey walls each create a completely different atmosphere, and understanding which suits your space is half the battle.

In small or north-facing rooms, I'd almost always steer towards mid-tones rather than very dark charcoal on the feature wall, unless you're intentionally going for that cosy, cocoon-like effect. In large, south-facing rooms with generous natural light, deep slate or near-black can look breathtaking.

Light vs dark grey feature wall: quick guide

  • Light grey feature wall: Suits small rooms, north-facing rooms, or spaces where you want it to feel fresh and open. Pairs beautifully with warm wood tones and blush or sage accents.
  • Dark grey / charcoal feature wall: Works brilliantly in large living rooms, main bedrooms, and dining rooms. Creates intimacy and drama — especially with warm lighting and metallic accents.
  • Medium grey feature wall: The safe middle ground — works in most rooms. Warm medium greys (a hint of beige or greige) are especially forgiving in rental properties.
  • Light grey on three walls, dark grey on feature wall: A classic contrast approach. This works particularly well behind a bed or sofa, where the deeper tone frames the furniture naturally.
  • All-dark-grey room: Can work, but only if you're very intentional about warm artificial lighting and varied textures to stop it reading as flat.

Here's something I tried in my own flat a few years back: I painted my bedroom feature wall in a deep charcoal, fully expecting to hate it after a week. Instead, with warm-toned bedside lighting and cream linen bedding, it became the best night's sleep of my life — the room felt like a proper retreat rather than a functional box. Sometimes you just have to try the scary option.

Pro Tip: If you're torn between light and dark grey, test both with large painted card samples before committing. Stick them on the wall and look at them at three different times of day: morning, early afternoon, and in the evening with lamps on. The evening result is usually the most revealing.

How to Style and Accessorize a Grey Feature Wall

Getting the feature wall treatment right is step one — but how you dress and style around it is what takes it from "nice paint job" to "properly designed room." A grey feature wall needs layering to feel finished, and layering is something most people don't do enough of.

Think in terms of three levels: the wall itself, the furniture against it, and the small objects and accessories that sit between them. When all three are considered together, the room stops looking like a showroom and starts looking like a home.

Accessorizing a grey feature wall: what to add layer by layer

  • Wall level: Mounted shelf, macramé hanging, round mirror, wall sconce lighting, or hanging plant — these add interest without committing to art on the wall.
  • Furniture level: Choose furniture that contrasts with grey — natural wood, warm rattan, cream or boucle upholstery. Avoid grey furniture against grey walls (it disappears).
  • Surface level: Ceramic vases, candles, sculptural objects, trailing plants — these add colour, texture, and personality at eye level and below.
  • Textiles: Throw cushions and blankets in warm tones (ochre, blush, terracotta, forest green) break up the grey and make the room feel lived-in.
  • Lighting: This is non-negotiable with grey. Warm-toned bulbs (2700K–3000K) in table and floor lamps stop grey from reading cold in the evenings.
Pro Tip: A round mirror on a grey feature wall does two things at once: it adds a decorative focal point and reflects light back into the room, making the grey feel warmer and less flat. It's one of the most reliable accessory choices I recommend for grey rooms.

Room-by-room grey feature wall tips

  • Bedroom: Go for the wall behind the bed (the headboard wall). Deep charcoal or warm mid-grey with soft linen bedding and warm lighting creates a genuinely restful atmosphere. Avoid very cold, blue-toned greys in a bedroom — they can feel clinical at night.
  • Living room: The chimney breast or the wall behind the sofa are your natural feature wall candidates. This is the room where you can be boldest — go darker, add panelling, or create a gallery wall with real personality. Warm metallic accents (brass, gold) are your friends here.
  • Hallway: Space is usually tight, so make a quick visual impact. A darker grey with a large round mirror and a statement pendant light is a classic combination that never dates. Keep the floor pale to compensate for the depth of colour.
  • Home office: A grey feature wall behind a desk is excellent for video calls (clean, professional backdrop) and also creates a sense of defined "work space" within a room. Add a pinboard, floating shelves, or a wall-mounted light to make it functional as well as good-looking.
  • Dining room: A charcoal or slate feature wall behind a dining table or sideboard creates the right amount of drama for evening meals. Pair with warm pendant lighting directly over the table.
Real Example: I worked with a client who had a narrow Victorian hallway with original dado rails — she wanted to make it feel special without spending a lot. We painted below the dado in deep slate grey and left the upper wall in a pale warm white, then added a gallery of small botanical prints above the dado rail. It looked like something from a design magazine and cost very little. The key was treating the dado rail as a natural dividing line rather than fighting it.

Common Mistakes to Avoid When Creating a Grey Room Feature Wall

I've seen the same mistakes made repeatedly over twelve years of advising on home decor — and most of them are very easy to avoid once you know what to look for. The biggest one? Choosing a feature wall that the room doesn't actually have a reason for. A feature wall needs a reason to exist: a sofa in front of it, a bed against it, a fireplace on it.

The second most common mistake is choosing the wrong grey. This sounds simple but it trips up almost everyone — grey has more undertones than almost any other colour family, and misreading those undertones is what causes rooms to look muddy, cold, or "off" despite using apparently nice colours.

Mistakes to avoid — the full list

  • Choosing a random wall: Always pick the wall that has a natural focal point in front of it — a sofa, a bed, a fireplace, a staircase.
  • Ignoring undertones: Mix warm-toned grey walls with cool-toned art or accessories and the room will never feel settled. Always identify your grey's undertone first.
  • Skipping warm lighting: Grey rooms NEED warm-toned artificial lighting. Cool white bulbs will make even the warmest grey feel bleak.
  • Matching furniture to the wall colour: Grey sofa against a grey wall disappears into itself. Use contrast — cream, warm wood, natural linen — to make both elements work.
  • Going too small with art: A single small print on a large grey feature wall looks like an afterthought. Scale up — go large or go gallery.
  • Using too many different frame colours: On a grey feature wall, inconsistent frames look chaotic. Pick one frame colour and stick to it throughout the wall.
  • Forgetting texture: Grey can be a very flat colour. Without textural contrast — in cushions, rugs, throws, ceramics — a grey feature wall reads dull rather than considered.
Pro Tip: The mistake I see most often is hanging art too high. On a grey feature wall, art should be hung so that the centre of the piece (or the centre of a gallery arrangement) sits at approximately eye level — around 145–150cm from the floor. When in doubt, go lower rather than higher.

How to Balance a Grey Feature Wall With the Rest of the Room Decor

A grey feature wall is only as good as the room that surrounds it — if the other three walls and the furniture feel disconnected from it, the feature wall just looks like a mistake. The goal is to make the feature wall feel intentional and anchored within the whole room, not like an isolated experiment.

The trick is to echo the feature wall's tones elsewhere in the room — not to repeat them exactly, but to reference them in smaller doses through accessories, textiles, and furniture choices.

How to balance your grey feature wall — practical steps

  • Keep the other three walls light: Off-white, warm white, or a very pale greige on the remaining walls will make the feature wall read as deliberate rather than overwhelming.
  • Echo the grey in accessories: A grey cushion on a cream sofa, a slate vase on a wood sideboard — these small touches link the feature wall to the rest of the room without repeating it.
  • Bring in a third colour: Grey and white alone can feel cold. Introduce a third tone — dusty pink, sage green, warm ochre — through soft furnishings to bring the room to life.
  • Keep the flooring contrasting: Light oak or pale rugs against a grey feature wall ground the room and stop the grey from pulling the space downward visually.
  • Use metallics to bridge the gap: Brass, copper, or warm gold accents in lighting and hardware sit comfortably against both grey and white, acting as a tonal bridge between the two.
Pro Tip: An easy rule I always use: if your feature wall is dark, keep at least 60% of the room light (walls, floor, main upholstery). If your feature wall is mid-tone, you have more freedom to add deeper tones in furniture and rugs without the room feeling heavy.

What the Experts Say About the Gray Feature Wall Trend

The gray feature wall has been a go-to choice for interior designers across the UK for well over a decade, and it shows no sign of going away — because it genuinely works.

What keeps the gray feature wall relevant is its adaptability. Unlike more prescriptive colour trends, grey shifts with the accessories around it — cool and contemporary one season, warm and earthy the next. It's one of the few choices that ages well precisely because it doesn't belong to a moment.

If you'd like a broader view of how designers are approaching this in living rooms specifically, I'd recommend having a look at this excellent round-up of Grey living room accent wall ideas from Ideal Home — there are some beautiful real-room examples there that complement what we've covered here. The underlying principles they discuss — contrast, texture, and tonal layering — are exactly what we've been working through in this guide.

What I'd add from my own experience is that the rooms that make the most of a grey feature wall tend to be the ones where the owner has thought about it as part of a whole room rather than as a standalone project. The wall is the foundation; everything else is the styling that makes it sing.

Ready to Create Your Feature Wall in a Grey Room?

I hope this guide has taken the guesswork out of one of the most common — and most rewarding — home styling projects there is. Whether you're going for a dramatic charcoal bedroom wall or a subtle mid-grey living room feature with a curated gallery of prints, the key is always the same: know your undertones, pick your focal point, layer your accessories, and get the lighting right.

The most important thing is to start. A feature wall doesn't have to be perfect on the first try — paint is remarkably fixable, art can be rehung, and accessories can be shuffled until they feel right. Give yourself permission to experiment.

So tell me — which room are you planning to tackle first, and are you leaning towards a paint treatment, wallpaper, panelling, or a gallery wall? I'd love to know what you're working with.

- No: high-gloss or shiny lacquered furniture, warm beige or cream tones, natural rattan or wicker, brass or gold metals, patterned upholstery, bright or saturated accent colours, rustic farmhouse elements
